```text
+/**
+ * The container must wrap (not be) an input with "maxlength", and supply the counter text via data attributes.
+ */
+export function initInputCharCounter(container: HTMLElement) {
+  const input = container.querySelector<HTMLInputElement | HTMLTextAreaElement>('input[maxlength], textarea[maxlength]');
+  if (!input) return;
+
+  const maxLength = Number(input.getAttribute('maxlength'));
+  const textForm1 = container.getAttribute('data-locale-chars-left-1')!;
+  const textFormN = container.getAttribute('data-locale-chars-left-n')!;
+
+  const counter = createElementFromAttrs<HTMLElement>('span', {class: 'input-char-counter'});
+  container.append(counter);
+
+  const updateCounter = () => {
+    // "maxlength" and JS string length both count UTF-16 code units, so they never disagree
+    const remaining = maxLength - input.value.length;
+    counter.textContent = trN(remaining, textForm1, textFormN);
+
+    counter.classList.toggle('near-limit', remaining <= 20 && remaining > 0);
+    counter.classList.toggle('at-limit', remaining <= 0);
+  };
+  updateCounter();
+  input.addEventListener('input', updateCounter);
+}
+
 export function initGlobalInput() {
   registerGlobalSelectorFunc('input, textarea', attachInputDirAuto);

   // It is useful for "New Issue"/"New PR" pages when the title is pre-filled with prefix text (e.g.: from template or commit message)

   registerGlobalInitFunc('autoFocusEnd', autoFocusEnd);
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-13 16:15:21Z)**_

All three new branches were pushed by teammate **abhoot** between Sept 10 and 12. None of them are merged into `main` yet.

---

### 1. `chore/claude-students-docs`: project documentation (Sept 10)
This is a documentation layer for finding your way around the Gitea codebase, aimed at both students and AI agents.

- **`.claude-students/`** (about 80 files):
  - `INDEX.md` maps each part of the code (models, modules, routers, services, templates, frontend, testing) to a short doc.
  - `docs/*.md` are the short reference docs.
  - `guide/*.md` are longer, beginner-friendly versions of the same topics, starting from `START-HERE.md`.
  - `README.md` and `MAINTENANCE.md` explain how the docs are organized and kept current, and `check.sh` validates them.
- **`AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`:** AI agents are now told to read `INDEX.md` first and open only the 1–3 docs that match the task. If you edit a `docs/*.md`, you also have to regenerate its `guide/*.md` twin, and you should run `check.sh` before pushing.
- **`.gitignore`:** adds `.specstory`.
- **AI session log:** one log is about 31,000 lines, which accounts for most of the branch's size.

Once this merges, the Claude setup in this repo will read those docs automatically.

### 2. `feat/issue-2-show-character-field`: title character counter (Sept 12)
This adds a "N characters left" counter under the issue title box. The box already has `maxlength="255"`.

- **`web_src/js/features/common-page.ts`:** a new reusable function, `initInputCharCounter`.
  - It finds an `<input>` or `<textarea>` with `maxlength` inside a container and adds a `<span>` after it.
  - The span updates on every keystroke. It uses the existing `trN` helper to choose between "character" and "characters."
  - The CSS classes `near-limit` (20 or fewer left) and `at-limit` (0 left) handle the styling.
  - It's registered with Gitea's `data-global-init` system, so any template can use it by adding an attribute.
- **Templates:** hooked into both the **New Issue** form (`new_form.tmpl`) and the **edit title** form on an existing issue (`view_title.tmpl`).
- **Locale:** adds `chars_left_1` and `chars_left_n` to `locale_en-US.json`. The template passes these strings to the JS through `data-locale-*` attributes, so the text stays translatable.
- **Other files:** new `char-counter.css`, vitest tests in `common-page.test.ts`, and an AI log.

**Note:** this branch already has `chore/claude-students-docs` merged into it. Merging it into `main` would bring in all the docs too.

### 3. `feat/issue-5-robots-txt`: default robots.txt (Sept 12)
Before this change, Gitea only served `/robots.txt` if an admin had created one in the `custom/` folder. This branch adds a built-in fallback.

- **`routers/web/misc/robots.txt`:** the default file. It blocks crawlers from URL patterns that are endless and useless for search, such as archives, blame, commits, compare, raw, RSS and activity. It deliberately leaves code, issues, pulls and the wiki crawlable.
- **`misc.go`:** the default file is built into the program with `//go:embed`. `RobotsTxt()` still checks `custom/public/robots.txt` first, then the older `custom/robots.txt`. If neither exists, it serves the built-in default.
- **`misc_test.go`:** tests that this order is respected, plus an AI log.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-13 16:55:49Z)**_

Yes, SQLite is fine, and it's usually the best choice for local development and class work:

- **Nothing extra to set up.** The whole database is a single file, so you don't need to install or run a separate MySQL or PostgreSQL server.
- **Gitea's own development setup uses it.** It's the default database for Gitea's integration tests (`make test-sqlite`), so it's well supported.
- **It's easy to reset.** Stop Gitea and delete the database file, and you're back to a clean install.

I checked `custom/conf/app.ini`. It has `DB_TYPE = sqlite3` on port 3000 with `ROOT_URL = http://localhost:3000/`, and the database file is `data/gitea.db`. Both `data/` and `custom/` are already in `.gitignore`, so your database and config (including the admin account) won't be committed.

The one real downside is that SQLite handles a lot of users writing at once poorly. That matters for a production server, not a local copy you're testing features on. The features you're working on, like the robots.txt or character counter branches, don't touch the database, so it doesn't matter which one you picked.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-13 16:56:19Z)**_

The tests are **in the code, and you run them from the terminal**. There's no button on the Gitea site for this. The Gitea server you just installed is only for trying out features by hand in the browser; the automated tests don't use it.

`STUDENTS.md` §6 lists the commands:

**Backend (Go) tests**
```bash
make test-backend          # unit tests
make test-integration      # integration tests (uses SQLite by default)
```

**Frontend (TypeScript) tests**
```bash
pnpm exec vitest run
```

To run just the tests for one change, which is much faster:
```bash
go test -run '^TestName$' ./routers/web/misc/          # one Go test
pnpm exec vitest web_src/js/features/common-page.test.ts   # one JS test file
```

The tests sit next to the code they check, in files ending in `_test.go` (Go) or `.test.ts` (TypeScript). The robots.txt branch, for example, adds `routers/web/misc/misc_test.go`.

**Watch out:** `STUDENTS.md` says to run the full test suite on **Linux, macOS, WSL2, or the devcontainer, not native Windows**. On Windows, a few unit tests fail for platform reasons (symlinks, cleaning up temp files) even when nothing is actually broken. Running one test for your own change is usually fine on Windows. For the full suite, use WSL2 so a Windows-only failure doesn't look like your bug.

You might also see a "run" button in two places, and neither is where you run these tests yourself:
- **GitHub pull requests:** tests may run automatically when you open a PR. That's a check after you push, not a replacement for running them locally.
- **The "Actions" tab on your Gitea site:** that's a feature Gitea offers its users, not the tests for Gitea's own code.

Yes, you need screenshots. Your Sprint 0 notes (saved in your `ai-logs` from Sept 3) list the evidence for **D1 – Project Setup (10 pts)** in the sprint report:
- a screenshot of the app running locally (Gitea at http://localhost:3000)
- a screenshot of the test suite passing

The report is due **Sept 17, 11:59 PM**. Also, "no app running (D1)" is one of the conditions that zeroes the whole sprint, so it's worth getting right.

**Don't screenshot the backend results yet, because they don't pass.** None of the failures are bugs in Gitea's code, and nobody has changed `main`. They come from how your WSL is set up.

### Results
| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Frontend (`pnpm exec vitest run`) | ✅ **46 files, 138 tests passed** (4s) |
| Backend (`make test-backend`) | ❌ **218 packages passed, 4 failed** (3 min) |

### Why the 4 backend packages failed
1. **Debian's Git is too old** (2.39.5). This causes 3 of the 4 package failures:
   - `modules/git` and `modules/gitrepo` test SHA-256 repositories, which Gitea only supports on Git ≥ 2.42.
   - `services/pull` uses `git merge-tree --merge-base`, and your Git reports "unknown option". That option first shipped in Git 2.40.
2. **Timezone** (`modules/git/pipeline`, `TestFindLFSFile`). The test compares times and fails on your New York timezone. Rerunning it with `TZ=UTC` made it pass.

### Fix
Debian 12's backports repository has a newer Git. Installing it needs your sudo password, so run it yourself in the prompt:

```
! wsl -d Debian -- bash -c "echo 'deb http://deb.debian.org/debian bookworm-backports main' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/backports.list && sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y -t bookworm-backports git"
```

After that, I'll rerun the backend tests with `TZ=UTC`, and they should all pass.

### Getting good screenshots
When the tests pass, run them yourself in a visible Debian terminal and screenshot the end of the output. The frontend summary shows "46 passed / 138 passed"; the backend run ends with a list of `ok` packages and no `FAIL`. My runs happen in the background, so there's no window for you to capture. I can give you the exact commands when you're ready. For the app screenshot, open http://localhost:3000 in your browser.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-13 17:37:38Z)**_

I was wrong about backports. Your install worked, but **Debian 12's backports repository doesn't carry a newer Git**. apt fell back to the regular `bookworm` package and only applied a security patch (`deb12u2` → `deb12u3`). You're still on 2.39.5, and the backend tests need ≥ 2.42.

The backports line you added is harmless, so you can leave it. To undo it: `sudo rm /etc/apt/sources.list.d/backports.list`.

Here's a fix that will actually work: **build a current Git from source into your home folder**. It only touches `~/git-sdk` and doesn't replace Debian's own Git. You'd undo it with `rm -rf ~/git-sdk`.

The only part that needs your password is installing the compiler and libraries. Run this in your Debian window:

```bash
sudo apt install -y build-essential libssl-dev zlib1g-dev libcurl4-gnutls-dev libexpat1-dev gettext
```

Tell me when it finishes. I'll then:
1. download the latest stable Git source from kernel.org and build it into `~/git-sdk`, which takes about 2–3 minutes and needs no sudo
2. put that Git first on the PATH for the test run only
3. rerun vitest and `make test-backend` with `TZ=UTC`, and print the output laid out like your Debian terminal

The alternative is upgrading the whole WSL install from Debian 12 to **Debian 13**, which ships Git 2.47. That's a bigger change to the system. Since this WSL is only for Gitea work, building Git from source is the smaller and easier-to-undo fix.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-13 22:16:07Z)**_

You're getting the same 4 failures as my first run, because that terminal is still using **the old Git (2.39.5) and your New York timezone**. The log shows it:

- `unknown option 'merge-base=...'` and `length 64 has no matched object format` are errors from the old Git.
- `-0500 EST` means `TZ=UTC` wasn't set.

So the `export PATH=... TZ=UTC` line didn't take effect in that window. Your Go also comes from `~/.local/go`, which is a different Go install than the one I used, so your shell sets up its own PATH. That's fine; the missing piece is putting Git 2.55 first.

Run this in the same Debian window:

```bash
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/git-sdk/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
git --version          # must say 2.55.0 — if it says 2.39.5, stop and tell me
cd ~/gitea
go clean -testcache
TZ=UTC make test-backend
```

- **The `~/.bashrc` line** makes the new Git permanent, so you won't need to re-export it in every new window.
- **`TZ=UTC` in front of `make`** applies UTC only to that one command, so your terminal's clock stays on your local time.
- **`go clean -testcache`** makes every package actually run instead of printing `(cached)`, which looks better in the screenshot.

The run should end with `ok      gitea.dev/tools`-style lines and no `FAIL` or `make: *** Error`. Your screen will also show the `?  ... [no test files]` lines, which I left out of my version. Those are normal and don't mean anything failed.

Here's a draft of the issue. It follows the D2 format from your Sprint 0 notes: title, summary, user story, scope and source, plus `scope:` and `type:` labels.

---

**Title:** Show a "stale" badge on branches with no recent commits

**Labels:** `type: feature`, `scope: small`

### Summary
The branch list (`/{owner}/{repo}/branches`) already shows when each branch was last updated, like "Updated 4 months ago". You still have to read every row to spot branches nobody is working on anymore. This feature adds a **"Stale" badge** next to any branch whose latest commit is older than a set number of days, so abandoned branches stand out at a glance.

This helps maintainers and teams keep the branch list clean. They can find and delete dead branches without checking commit dates one by one.

### User story
As a repository maintainer, I want branches with no recent commits flagged as stale so that I can quickly find and clean up abandoned branches.

### Proposed behavior
- A branch gets a **Stale** badge if its latest commit is older than the threshold.
- **Default threshold:** 90 days. An instance admin can change it in `app.ini` (e.g. `[repository.branch] STALE_BRANCH_DAYS = 90`), and `0` turns the feature off.
- Hovering the badge shows a tooltip such as "No commits in 90+ days".
- These branches never get the badge:
  - the default branch
  - deleted branches, which already show "Deleted by…"
- The badge is only visual. It doesn't delete, block or change any branch.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Branches older than the threshold show a Stale badge on the branches page.
- [ ] Branches newer than the threshold, the default branch and deleted branches don't show it.
- [ ] The threshold can be set in `app.ini`, and `0` turns the badge off.
- [ ] The badge text and tooltip are translatable, with keys in `locale_en-US.json`.
- [ ] A unit test covers the stale / not stale / disabled cases.

### Implementation notes
- Each branch's last commit time is already loaded as `DBBranch.CommitTime` (`models/git/branch.go:119`) and shown in `templates/repo/branch/list.tmpl:109`. No new database fields or git calls are needed.
- The new setting would go in `modules/setting/repository.go`.
- The badge can reuse the existing `ui label` style that the page already uses for PR status labels.

### Rough scope
**Small.** The data already exists, so the work is one setting, one template change, two locale strings and a unit test, well within 1–1.5 weeks.

### Source
Personal use and our own team workflow. Our fork is building up feature branches, and it's hard to tell which ones are abandoned.

---

```markdown
## Summary
The branch list (`/{owner}/{repo}/branches`) already shows when each branch was last updated ("Updated 4 months ago"), but you have to read every row to spot branches nobody is working on anymore. This feature adds a **"Stale" badge** next to any branch whose latest commit is older than a set number of days, so abandoned branches stand out at a glance.

This helps maintainers and teams keep the branch list clean: they can find and delete dead branches without checking commit dates one by one.

## User story
As a repository maintainer, I want branches with no recent commits flagged as stale so that I can quickly find and clean up abandoned branches.

## Proposed behavior
- A branch gets a **Stale** badge if its latest commit is older than the threshold.
- **Default threshold:** 90 days. An instance admin can change it in `app.ini` (e.g. `[repository.branch] STALE_BRANCH_DAYS = 90`); `0` turns the feature off.
- Hovering the badge shows a tooltip such as "No commits in 90+ days".
- These branches never get the badge:
  - the default branch
  - deleted branches, which already show "Deleted by…"
- The badge is only visual. It doesn't delete, block, or change any branch.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Branches older than the threshold show a Stale badge on the branches page.
- [ ] Branches newer than the threshold, the default branch, and deleted branches don't show it.
- [ ] The threshold can be set in `app.ini`, and `0` turns the badge off.
- [ ] The badge text and tooltip are translatable, with keys in `locale_en-US.json`.
- [ ] A unit test covers the stale / not stale / disabled cases.

## Implementation notes
- Each branch's last commit time is already loaded as `DBBranch.CommitTime` (`models/git/branch.go`) and shown in `templates/repo/branch/list.tmpl`. No new database fields or git calls are needed.
- The new setting would go in `modules/setting/repository.go`.
- The badge can reuse the existing `ui label` style that the page already uses for PR status labels.

## Rough scope
**Small.** The data already exists, so the work is one setting, one template change, two locale strings, and a unit test — well within 1–1.5 weeks.

## Source
Personal use and our own team workflow. Our fork is building up feature branches, and it's hard to tell which ones are abandoned.

---
```

I checked the codebase, and Gitea has no close reasons today: there's no `close_reason` or `state_reason` anywhere in the models, API structs or templates. So this is a real new feature. I also traced every place an issue gets closed, so the auto-close part of the issue can list each path.

Here's the draft:

---

**Title:** Let users choose a reason when closing an issue (Completed, Not planned, Duplicate)

**Labels:** `type/feature`, `scope: large`, `enhancement`

### Summary
In Gitea, a closed issue is simply "closed." There's no way to tell whether it was fixed, rejected, or a duplicate of another issue. Maintainers end up writing "closing as duplicate of #12" in comments, and anyone looking at the closed-issues list later can't tell finished work from abandoned ideas.

This feature adds a **close reason** that's chosen when an issue is closed and saved in the database. The reason appears on the issue and in its timeline. Issues closed automatically, for example by a commit or a merged PR, get a sensible reason too.

It helps maintainers triage faster. It also helps contributors and project managers read a project's history accurately; for example, how much was actually completed versus declined.

### User story
As a repository maintainer, I want to choose why I'm closing an issue (completed, not planned, or duplicate) so that anyone reading the issue later knows what happened to it without digging through comments.

### Proposed behavior
**Closing manually (web UI)**
- The **Close issue** button becomes a split button with a dropdown: **Close as completed** (default), **Close as not planned**, **Close as duplicate**.
- **Duplicate** asks for the original issue number (e.g. `#12`), which is saved and linked.
- The **issue list** bulk "Close" action gets the same reason choice.

**Saving and display**
- The reason is stored on the issue in a new database column, added through a migration. For duplicates, the original issue's ID is stored too.
- The timeline entry changes from "closed this issue" to e.g. "closed this as not planned" or "closed this as a duplicate of #12".
- Closed issues show a matching icon or label, so "not planned" looks different from "completed."
- **Reopening** an issue clears the reason.
- Existing closed issues keep no reason and display exactly as they do today.

**Automatic closing**

| How the issue closes | Code path | Reason saved |
|---|---|---|
| Commit message keyword ("fixes #5") | `services/issue/commit.go` | Completed |
| PR merged that references the issue | `services/pull/merge.go` | Completed |
| PR closed when its branch is deleted or its target is removed | `services/pull/pull.go` | Not planned |
| API call without a reason | `routers/api/v1/repo/issue.go` | Completed (default) |

**API**
- `PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{index}` accepts an optional `close_reason` field (`completed`, `not_planned`, `duplicate`) plus `duplicate_of`.
- The issue JSON response includes `close_reason`, similar to GitHub's `state_reason`.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A database migration adds the close-reason columns, and existing issues are unaffected.
- [ ] Users can pick a reason from the Close button on the issue page and from the bulk close action on the issue list.
- [ ] Duplicate requires a valid issue number in the same repository, and the timeline links to it.
- [ ] The timeline and closed-issue display show the reason, with all text translatable in `locale_en-US.json`.
- [ ] Commit-keyword and merged-PR closes save **Completed**, and the other automatic paths save the reason in the table above.
- [ ] Reopening clears the reason.
- [ ] The API accepts and returns `close_reason`.
- [ ] Unit tests cover the model/service logic for each reason and each automatic path, plus a migration test.

### Implementation notes

```markdown
## Summary
In Gitea, a closed issue or pull request is simply "closed" — there's no way to tell whether it was fixed, rejected, a duplicate, or closed for some other reason. Maintainers end up writing "closing as duplicate of #12" in comments, and anyone browsing closed items later can't tell finished work from abandoned ideas.

This feature adds a **close reason** to issues and pull requests. The reason is chosen when closing, saved in the database, and shown on the issue/PR and in its timeline. Preset reasons cover the common cases, and an **Other** option lets the user type a custom reason. Items closed automatically (by a commit, a merged PR, a deleted branch, etc.) get a sensible reason too.

This helps maintainers triage faster, and helps contributors and project managers read a project's history accurately — for example, how much was actually completed versus declined.

## User story
As a repository maintainer, I want to choose why I'm closing an issue or pull request — from a list or by typing my own reason — so that anyone reading it later knows what happened without digging through comments.

## Proposed behavior

### Closing manually (web UI)
- The **Close** button on issues becomes a split button with a dropdown:
  - **Close as completed** (default)
  - **Close as not planned**
  - **Close as duplicate** — asks for the original issue number (e.g. `#12`)
  - **Close with other reason…** — shows a text box for a custom reason (required when chosen, max 255 characters)
- The **Close pull request** button gets the same dropdown **without "Completed"**, since a finished PR is *merged*, not closed. Options: **Not planned** (default), **Duplicate**, **Other…**. Merging stays a separate state and needs no reason.
- The **issue/PR list** bulk "Close" action offers the same reason choice (preset reasons only; one reason applied to all selected items).

### Saving and display
- A database migration adds to the `issue` table (which also stores PRs):
  - `close_reason` — `completed`, `not_planned`, `duplicate`, or `other`
  - `close_reason_text` — the custom text when the reason is `other`
  - `duplicate_of_id` — the original issue/PR when the reason is `duplicate`
- The same fields are stored on the close timeline comment, so every close/reopen in the history keeps its own reason.
- The timeline shows e.g. "closed this as not planned", "closed this as a duplicate of #12", or "closed this: *custom text*".
- Custom text is displayed as plain text (escaped, not rendered as Markdown/HTML).
- Closed items show a distinct icon/label per reason (e.g. "not planned" looks different from "completed").
- **Reopening** clears the current reason (the old reason stays visible in the timeline).
- Existing closed issues/PRs have no reason and display exactly as they do today.

### Automatic closing

| How it closes | Code path | Reason saved |
|---|---|---|
| Commit message keyword ("fixes #5") | `services/issue/commit.go` | Completed |
| Merged PR that references an issue | `services/pull/merge.go` | Completed (on the referenced issue) |
| PR auto-closed because its head branch was deleted | `services/pull/pull.go` (`AdjustPullsCausedByBranchDeleted`) | Not planned |
| PRs auto-closed because the repo's branches were removed | `services/pull/pull.go` (`CloseRepoBranchesPulls`) | Not planned |
| API call that closes without giving a reason | `routers/api/v1/repo/issue.go` | Completed (issues) / Not planned (PRs) |

### API
- Issue and pull request edit endpoints accept optional `close_reason` (`completed`, `not_planned`, `duplicate`, `other`), `close_reason_text`, and `duplicate_of` fields.
- Issue and PR JSON responses include `close_reason` and `close_reason_text` (similar to GitHub's `state_reason`).
- Invalid combinations are rejected with 422 (e.g. `other` with empty text, `duplicate` pointing at a nonexistent issue, `completed` on a PR).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A database migration adds the close-reason columns; existing issues and PRs are unaffected.
- [ ] Users can pick a preset reason or type a custom one when closing an issue or PR from its page.
- [ ] PRs do not offer "Completed"; merging still works without a reason.
- [ ] The bulk close action on issue/PR lists lets users pick a preset reason.
- [ ] "Duplicate" requires a valid issue/PR number in the same repository, and the timeline links to it.
- [ ] "Other" requires non-empty text (≤ 255 chars), which is saved and displayed escaped.
- [ ] Timeline and closed-item display show the reason; all new UI strings are in `locale_en-US.json`.
- [ ] Each automatic close path saves the reason listed in the table above.
- [ ] Reopening clears the current reason but keeps it in the timeline history.
- [ ] The API accepts, validates, and returns the close-reason fields for issues and PRs.
- [ ] Unit tests cover each reason, custom-text validation, each automatic path, and the migration.

## Implementation notes
- Every close goes through `issues_model.SetIssueAsClosed` (`models/issues/issue_update.go:51`), which currently only updates `is_closed` and `closed_unix`. The reason would be added there and passed down from `issue_service.CloseIssue` (`services/issue/status.go:17`) by each caller.
- Web routes: `routers/web/repo/issue_comment.go` (Close button) and `routers/web/repo/issue_list.go` (bulk close).
- Timeline close events are `CommentTypeClose` (`models/issues/comment.go:71`).
- Close button template: `templates/repo/issue/view_content.tmpl`.
- Possible follow-up: Gitea's GitHub migration test data already contains GitHub's `state_reason`, so a later issue could import close reasons when migrating from GitHub.

## Rough scope
**Large.** It touches every layer of Gitea — a database migration, the issue/PR model and services, several automatic-close paths, web UI in two places with custom-text input, the REST API, and tests — more than a single sprint of work.

## Source
Personal use and a feature gap compared to GitHub, which supports "Close as completed / not planned / duplicate". Our own team's tracker would benefit, since the current closed state can't tell finished work from declined work.
```

I'd make this your **ambitious (Large)** issue. It's more work than it looks, but it's a good fit for that slot.

### Why it's Large
**1. Gitea doesn't store history.** A milestone only keeps its *current* counts (`NumIssues`, `NumClosedIssues` in `models/issues/milestone.go:55`). There's no record of how many issues were open last Tuesday. You'd have to rebuild that from each issue's timeline:
- when the issue was created
- close and reopen events
- milestone changes. A `CommentTypeMilestone` comment (`models/issues/comment.go:79`) records both the old and new milestone, so you can tell when an issue was added to or moved out of a milestone.

Replaying those events correctly is the hard part, and it has edge cases:
- an issue added to the milestone after it was already closed
- an issue moved between milestones
- an issue reopened several times
- a milestone with no due date, or whose due date changed

**2. It spans the full stack.** You'd need a backend query to rebuild the counts, a new route or API endpoint to serve the data, a new chart component, UI wiring and tests.

**3. The chart itself is the easy part.** Gitea already uses **Chart.js** in three Vue components (`RepoContributors.vue`, `RepoCodeFrequency.vue`, `RepoRecentCommits.vue`). You can copy their pattern, and the "ideal" line is just a straight line from the starting count to 0 at the due date.

A small/medium version would only be possible if you skipped history, for example by recording a daily snapshot from now on. The chart would then be empty for every existing milestone, which weakens the feature.

### Choosing between your two ideas
I'd **combine them** into one issue, because they share the hard part:
- **Main feature: a milestone burndown chart** on the milestone page, from the creation date to the due date, with the ideal line.
- **Second view: open issues over time for the whole repository**, using the same rebuilt data without the milestone filter.

For where the repository chart goes, consider Gitea's **Activity** tab instead of the Issues tab. Activity already holds the Contributors, Code Frequency and Recent Commits charts, so a new "Issues" sub-tab there would match the UI. Adding a chart tab under Issues would be a new pattern for Gitea.

Combining them also makes the issue obviously ambitious. If a teammate implements it and runs short on time, the milestone chart is the natural stopping point, and the repository view can become a follow-up.

Want me to draft it that way: Large, milestone burndown plus a repository-wide chart under Activity? And do you want the chart limited to **issues**, or should PRs in the milestone count too?

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-13 22:54:44Z)**_

Both views count open issues over time using the same rebuilt history. They differ in which issues count, what time range they cover, and what question they answer.

| | **Milestone burndown** | **Repository issues chart (Activity tab)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Question it answers** | "Will we finish this milestone by the due date?" | "Is our backlog growing or shrinking over time?" |
| **Where it lives** | On the milestone's page (`/milestone/{id}`) | New sub-tab under **Activity**, next to Contributors / Code Frequency |
| **Which issues count** | Only issues **assigned to that milestone**, including issues added or removed partway through | **All** issues in the repository |
| **Time range** | Fixed: milestone **creation → due date**, extended to today if overdue | User-chosen: last month / 3 months / year / all time |
| **Ideal line** | ✅ A straight line from the starting count down to 0 on the due date | ❌ There's no finish line to aim at, so an ideal line doesn't make sense |
| **Lines on the chart** | Open issues (actual) vs. ideal | Open issues over time, plus opened and closed per week, so you can see *why* the count changed |
| **Typical user** | A team lead checking a sprint (like your course sprints) | A maintainer checking overall project health |
| **Edge cases** | Issues moving in and out of the milestone; milestone with no due date (no ideal line); due date changed | Only creation, close and reopen events matter, since milestones are ignored |

### How they relate
- The repository chart is the **simpler** one. It only replays created, closed and reopened events for every issue.
- The milestone chart is the **same replay plus a filter**. It also has to track when each issue joined or left the milestone, which is where most of the tricky cases are.

So one backend function could power both, something like `OpenIssueCountsOverTime(repo, milestone (optional), from, to)`. With no milestone it gives the repository chart; with one it gives the burndown. On the frontend, both can be a single Chart.js component with an optional ideal line.

That's why they belong in **one issue**. The shared history rebuild is most of the work, and each view adds a smaller amount on top.

You could also point out the connection to your class: your team runs fixed-length sprints, and the milestone burndown is exactly the chart a scrum team would use to track one.

Want me to draft it? One question is still open: should the chart count only **issues**, or should **pull requests** in the milestone count too? I'd suggest issues only by default, with an "include pull requests" toggle.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-13 22:55:56Z)**_

Yes, and it can be split cleanly if each issue stands on its own and the ambitious one keeps enough substance to earn "ambitious." Here's how I'd divide them.

### Small/medium: Activity tab "Issues" chart
**Scope: medium.** The simple version is doable in 1–1.5 weeks, because it can skip replaying the full timeline:
- An issue was open at time *t* if it was created before *t* and either isn't closed or was closed after *t*.
- Both dates are already stored on each issue (`created_unix`, `closed_unix`), so a single query covers it.
- The Activity tab already has Chart.js pages (Contributors, Code Frequency, Recent Commits) to copy.
- Views: open issues over time, plus opened and closed per week, with a time-range picker.

**Known limitation, stated in the issue:** an issue that was closed and later reopened only keeps its latest close date. Its past closed periods won't show on the chart. That's an accepted approximation for this version.

### Ambitious: Milestone burndown chart
**Scope: large.** To keep it from looking like "the medium chart plus a filter," give it the parts that are actually hard:
- **Accurate history rebuild.** Replay the timeline comments (close, reopen, milestone added/removed/moved), so reopened issues and issues moving between milestones are counted correctly.
- **Ideal line** from the starting count to 0 at the due date.
- **Scope-change markers:** show when issues were added to or removed from the milestone mid-sprint. That's often why a burndown goes *up*.
- **Projected finish date,** a trend line from the current burn rate: "at this pace, done on Oct 3."
- **Hover details** listing which issues closed or were added on each day.
- **Edge cases:** no due date, due date changed, overdue milestone.

### Keep them independent
The course says teammates implement each other's issues and no two members can take the same issue, so these may be built by **different people in any order**. I'd write them so:
- Neither issue *requires* the other.
- The burndown issue says: "if the Activity issues chart has already merged, reuse its chart component."

### A risk to know about
A grader could see the burndown as "the same chart again" if the ambitious issue doesn't make its additions clear. The accurate timeline replay, scope-change markers and projected finish date are what separate it, so the issue should explain them clearly.

With these two, your D2 set would be complete:

| Issue | Slot |
|---|---|
| #11 Stale branch badge | small/medium |
| Activity tab issues chart | small/medium |
| #12 Close reasons | ambitious |
| Milestone burndown chart | ambitious |

Want me to draft both? The earlier question is still open: **issues only**, or an "include pull requests" toggle? I'd suggest issues only for the Activity chart, to keep it medium, and a toggle on the burndown.

```markdown
## Summary
Gitea's **Activity** tab has charts for Contributors, Code Frequency, and Recent Commits, but nothing for issues. There's no way to see whether a project's backlog is growing or shrinking — only the current number of open issues.

This feature adds an **Issues** sub-tab under Activity with a chart of **open issues over time**, plus the number of issues **opened and closed per week**, so maintainers can see trends and why the count changed.

It helps maintainers and project leads judge project health at a glance (e.g. "we're closing issues faster than they're opened") and helps contributors see how actively issues are handled.

## User story
As a repository maintainer, I want to see how the number of open issues has changed over time so that I can tell whether our backlog is growing or shrinking and react early.

## Proposed behavior
- New sub-tab **Activity → Issues** at `/{owner}/{repo}/activity/issues`, next to Contributors / Code Frequency / Recent Commits.
- Only shown when the repository has the Issues unit enabled.
- The chart shows:
  - **Open issues** over time (line)
  - **Opened per week** and **closed per week** (bars)
- **Time range picker:** last month, last 3 months, last year, all time (default: last 3 months).
- Hovering a point shows the date and its values.
- **Issues only** — pull requests are not counted.
- Empty state message when the repository has no issues.

### How counts are calculated
An issue is counted as open at time *t* if it was created before *t* and is either still open or was closed after *t*. This uses the `created_unix` and `closed_unix` values already stored on every issue, so no timeline replay or new database columns are needed.

**Known limitation (accepted for this issue):** an issue that was closed and later reopened only keeps its most recent close date, so its earlier closed periods aren't reflected. Accurate history from timeline events is out of scope here.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] An **Issues** sub-tab appears under Activity when the Issues unit is enabled, and is hidden otherwise.
- [ ] The chart shows open issues over time plus opened/closed per week.
- [ ] The time range picker updates the chart.
- [ ] Pull requests are excluded from all counts.
- [ ] Users without permission to read issues cannot see the page or its data endpoint.
- [ ] All new UI strings are in `locale_en-US.json`.
- [ ] Unit tests cover the count calculation (open, closed, closed after the range, empty repo).

## Implementation notes
- Follow the existing Activity sub-tabs: each is a page route plus a `/data` JSON endpoint (`routers/web/web.go:1608-1618`, e.g. `routers/web/repo/contributors.go`), linked from `templates/repo/navbar.tmpl`.
- The frontend can copy the Chart.js pattern from `web_src/js/components/RepoCodeFrequency.vue` / `RepoContributors.vue`.
- Weekly buckets can be computed in one query over the repo's issues (`is_pull = false`) using `created_unix` and `closed_unix`.

## Rough scope
**Medium.** It follows an existing page + data-endpoint + Chart.js pattern and needs no schema changes, but it adds a new route, a query, a Vue chart component, permissions, and tests — about 1–1.5 weeks.

## Source
Personal use and our team's workflow: we run fixed-length sprints and want to see whether our issue backlog is trending in the right direction. Related to the milestone burndown chart issue, but independent — neither requires the other.

---
```

```markdown
## Summary
A Gitea milestone page shows only a progress bar and the current open/closed counts. There's no way to see how work progressed over the milestone's life, whether the team is on track for the due date, or when scope was added mid-way.

This feature adds a **burndown chart** to the milestone page: the number of open issues from the milestone's **creation to its due date**, compared against an **ideal line**, with markers for scope changes and a **projected finish date** based on the current pace.

It helps teams running sprints or releases (like our own course sprints) spot early when a milestone is slipping, and helps leads explain *why* — for example, because issues were added partway through.

## User story
As a team lead, I want a burndown chart for each milestone comparing actual progress against an ideal pace so that I can tell early whether we'll finish by the due date and see when scope changed.

## Proposed behavior

### Chart
Shown on the milestone page (`/{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}`) above the issue list, collapsible.

- **X-axis:** milestone creation date → due date (extended to today if the milestone is overdue).
- **Actual line:** number of open items in the milestone at the end of each day.
- **Ideal line:** a straight line from the open count at the milestone's start down to 0 at the due date.
- **Scope-change markers:** points where items were **added to** or **removed from** the milestone (explains why the actual line goes *up*).
- **Projected finish:** a dashed trend line from the recent burn rate, with a label such as "At this pace: Oct 3". Hidden when there's not enough data or nothing has closed yet.
- **Hover details:** for each day, list which items were closed, reopened, added, or removed (with links).
- **Include pull requests toggle:** off by default (issues only); when on, PRs in the milestone are counted too. The choice is kept in the URL (e.g. `?include_pulls=1`) so it can be shared.

### Accurate history
Counts are rebuilt by replaying each item's timeline, not from the current state:
- issue created (only counts once it's in the milestone)
- closed (`CommentTypeClose`) and reopened (`CommentTypeReopen`) events
- milestone changes (`CommentTypeMilestone`, which records the old and new milestone), so items moved between milestones are counted only while they belonged to this one
- merged PRs count as closed when the pull request toggle is on

### Edge cases
- **No due date:** show the actual line and scope markers from creation to today; hide the ideal line and projection, with a note explaining why.
- **Due date changed:** use the current due date for the ideal line.
- **Overdue milestone:** extend the X-axis to today; the ideal line still ends at the due date.
- **Closed milestone:** the chart ends at the milestone's close date.
- **Item added after it was already closed:** changes the total but not the open count.
- **Empty milestone:** show an empty-state message instead of a chart.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The milestone page shows a burndown chart from creation to due date with actual and ideal lines.
- [ ] History is rebuilt from timeline events, so reopened items and items moved between milestones are counted correctly.
- [ ] Scope additions and removals are marked on the chart.
- [ ] A projected finish date is shown when there's enough data, and hidden otherwise.
- [ ] Hovering a day lists the items that changed that day.
- [ ] The "Include pull requests" toggle is off by default, changes the counts when turned on, and is reflected in the URL.
- [ ] All edge cases above behave as described.
- [ ] Users without permission to read the milestone's issues/PRs cannot see the chart or its data endpoint, and private items are never leaked in hover details.
- [ ] All new UI strings are in `locale_en-US.json`.
- [ ] Unit tests cover the timeline replay (close/reopen, add/remove/move between milestones, add-after-closed, PR toggle) and the ideal/projection calculations.

## Implementation notes
- Milestone dates are on `models/issues/milestone.go` (`CreatedUnix`, `DeadlineUnix`, `ClosedDateUnix`); it currently stores only current counts (`NumIssues`, `NumClosedIssues`), so history must come from comments.
- Timeline event types are defined in `models/issues/comment.go` (`CommentTypeReopen` = 1, `CommentTypeClose` = 2, `CommentTypeMilestone` = 8, with `OldMilestoneID` / `MilestoneID`).
- Milestone page: `routers/web/repo/milestone.go` (`MilestoneIssuesAndPulls`) and `templates/repo/issue/milestone_issues.tmpl`. A JSON data endpoint like the Activity charts' `/data` routes (`routers/web/web.go:1608-1618`) keeps page load fast.
- Frontend can follow the Chart.js pattern in `web_src/js/components/RepoCodeFrequency.vue` / `RepoContributors.vue`.
- Related to #13 (Activity tab issues chart) but **independent** — neither requires the other. If #13 has already merged, reuse its chart component where it fits.

## Rough scope
**Large.** The core is an accurate timeline-replay engine across close, reopen, and milestone-move events, plus scope-change detection, projection math, a PR toggle, many edge cases, permission checks, a new data endpoint, a chart UI, and thorough tests — more than a single sprint of work.

## Source
Personal use and our team's workflow: we plan work in fixed-length sprints with due dates, and a burndown chart is the standard way scrum teams track whether a sprint is on track. Also a gap compared to tools like Jira and GitLab, which offer milestone burndown charts.

---
*Drafted with Claude Code (Opus 5) for @CarsonRackley.*
```

```text
  Create or update markdown files for the agent sessions in the current working directory.

  USAGE  
         
    specstory sync [provider-id] [--flags]                                
            
  EXAMPLES  
            
    # Sync all agents with activity

    specstory sync claude

    specstory sync copilotide                                             
    specstory sync cursor                                                 
    specstory sync cursoride                                              
    specstory sync deepseek                                               
    specstory sync droid

    # Sync multiple sessions                                              
    specstory sync -s <session-id-1> -s <session-id-2> -s <session-id-3>  
                                                                          
    # Output session markdown to stdout without saving

    # Output multiple sessions to stdout

    # Sync all sessions for the current directory, with console output

    # Sync all sessions for the current directory, with a log file

  FLAGS  
         
    --config-dir              Custom directory for the project-level config.toml (default: ./.specstory/cli)
    --console                 Enable error/warn/info output to stdout
    --debug                   Enable debug-level output (requires --console or --log)
    --debug-dir               Custom output directory for debug data (default: ./.specstory/debug)
    -h --help                 Help for sync
    --local-time-zone         Use local timezone for file name and content timestamps (when not present: UTC)
    --log                     Write error/warn/info output to ./.specstory/debug/debug.log
    --no-cloud-sync           Disable cloud sync functionality

    --no-usage-analytics      Disable usage analytics
    --no-version-check        Skip checking for newer versions
    --only-cloud-sync         Skip local markdown file saves, only upload to cloud (requires authentication)
    --only-stats              Only update statistics, skip local markdown files and cloud sync
    --output-dir              Custom output directory for markdown files (default: ./.specstory/history)
```
